name: Amazon EKS
summary: AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you; you choose how much of the worker side to hand over too.
intro: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) runs upstream, certified-conformant Kubernetes. When you create a cluster, AWS starts its control plane in an account it owns: at least two API server instances and three etcd instances spread over three Availability Zones, replaced automatically if one fails. You get an API endpoint and pay a flat fee per cluster. The worker nodes live in your own VPC, and the VPC CNI plugin gives every Pod a real private IP address from that VPC, so Pods talk to other AWS resources without an overlay network.

What varies is who runs the nodes. With self-managed nodes you launch and patch EC2 instances yourself. Managed node groups wrap an EC2 Auto Scaling group that EKS creates, updates and drains for you. Fargate runs each Pod in its own isolated compute boundary with no node to see at all. EKS Auto Mode (December 2024) goes furthest: AWS picks and launches instances with Karpenter, runs core add-ons such as networking, storage and load balancing, and replaces every node at least every 21 days. Karpenter on its own sits in between: you install it, and it launches right-sized EC2 instances for Pods that are waiting.
strengths: No etcd or API servers to run, back up or upgrade: AWS spreads them over three Availability Zones
Pods get VPC IP addresses and per-Pod IAM roles, so security groups, load balancers and IAM policies work as they do for EC2
A range of node options in one cluster: self-managed, managed node groups, Fargate, Auto Mode, and on-premises hybrid nodes
Same upstream Kubernetes as everywhere else; EKS Distro publishes the exact builds EKS uses
limits: The $0.10 per hour cluster fee (about $73 a month) is paid before any workload runs, and rises to $0.60 per hour once a version leaves standard support
A Kubernetes version gets 14 months of standard support; stay longer and you pay extended support, and after 26 months EKS upgrades the control plane for you
Fargate Pods can’t run DaemonSets, privileged containers or GPUs, and can’t mount EBS volumes
Auto Mode adds a per-instance management fee on top of the EC2 price, and its nodes can’t be reached by SSH or use custom AMIs

story: By 2017, many AWS customers were already running Kubernetes on EC2 themselves; AWS quoted a CNCF figure that 63% of Kubernetes workloads ran on AWS. Doing it well meant running at least three Kubernetes masters in different Availability Zones, wiring them to share state and fail over, and then patching and upgrading them and the workers. Customers asked AWS to make that easier, and a month earlier Microsoft had announced its own managed service, AKS.

AWS announced Amazon Elastic Container Service for Kubernetes as a preview at re:Invent on November 29, 2017, promising upstream Kubernetes with a multi-zone control plane. It became generally available on June 5, 2018, at $0.20 per cluster per hour, with worker nodes you launched and managed yourself. Over the next few years AWS took over more of the data plane: managed node groups in November 2019, Fargate for EKS Pods in December 2019, the open-source Karpenter autoscaler in 2021, and EKS Auto Mode in December 2024, which manages the nodes too.

In January 2020 AWS halved the cluster fee to $0.10 per hour. In 2023 it added extended support so that clusters could stay on an old Kubernetes version for an extra year, priced at $0.60 per hour from April 2024. AWS also took EKS outside its cloud: EKS Distro (December 2020) publishes the Kubernetes builds EKS uses, and EKS Anywhere (September 2021) runs clusters on VMware vSphere, bare metal and other on-premises hardware.

choices.choice: Run upstream Kubernetes, not a fork
choices.why: AWS said customers wanted to use existing Kubernetes plugins and tools unchanged. EKS is certified conformant, so workloads move between EKS and other clusters without changes.

choices.choice: A control plane spread over three Availability Zones
choices.why: A cluster whose API server or etcd fails can’t schedule or heal anything. Spreading them over three zones lets a cluster survive the loss of one.

choices.choice: Pod IP addresses straight from the VPC
choices.why: The VPC CNI plugin attaches network interfaces to each node and gives Pods VPC addresses, so security groups, routing and load balancers treat a Pod like any other machine in the network, with no overlay network in between.

choices.choice: Hand over the nodes one step at a time
choices.why: At launch you ran your own worker nodes. Managed node groups, Fargate, Karpenter and then Auto Mode each took more of that work away, while self-managed nodes stayed available for teams that need full control.

Generally available on June 5, at $0.20 per cluster per hour
Managed node groups in November; Fargate support in December
